lifeTables.source: Siler-type model (falling infant hazard + constant background + Gompertz old-age hazard) fitted to e0 27, q0 0.22, 5q0 0.37. Cf. Gurven & Kaplan 2007 forager life tables (e0 21-37, modal adult death age ~70) and Coale-Demeny West levels 3-4. Early farming (Neolithic) populations were likely at the low end.

Same model fitted to e0 26, q0 0.28, 5q0 0.45. Cf. Frier's Roman life table (~Coale-Demeny West level 3, e0 ~25), Roman Egypt census returns (Bagnall & Frier 1994) and Bronze Age skeletal series. Maternal mortality kept the female advantage small.
Model fitted to e0 30 (range roughly 25-35; plague decades after 1347 were far worse). Cf. Coale-Demeny West level 5 and medieval English estimates (Russell, Hollingsworth).

Model fitted to e0 33, q0 0.21. Cf. Wrigley & Schofield reconstruction for England (e0 ~32-40), French parish reconstitutions (~25-30 in the 1700s) and Qing China estimates; Coale-Demeny West ~level 6.
Model fitted to e0 35. World e0 ~29-30 (Riley 2005); England and Wales ~40, USA ~38-40, India and China ~25-30. Blended toward the European, US and Chinese streams drawn in the blue layer.
Model fitted to e0 40, q0 0.16. World e0 ~32 in 1900 and ~34 in 1913 (Riley 2005); USA ~47, western Europe ~45-50, India and China ~24-30. Blended.
Model fitted to e0 50, q0 0.13. World e0 ~46 in 1950 (UN WPP 2024), female advantage ~4; USA ~68, western Europe ~65, China and India roughly 35-45. Blended.

Model fitted to e0 62. World e0 ~58 in 1975 (UN WPP 2024); USA ~72.6, western Europe ~72, China ~62, India ~50. World female advantage ~4.4 years; it peaked near 8 years in the USA (late 1970s) and about 10 in the USSR.
Model fitted to e0 69. World e0 ~66 in 2000 (UN WPP 2024), female advantage ~4.9; USA ~76.8, EU ~77, China ~71, India ~62. Russia's female advantage was ~13 years.
Model fitted to e0 74. World e0 72.6 in 2019, ~71 in 2021 (COVID-19), 73.2 in 2023 (UN WPP 2024); USA ~78.8 (2019); UN medium projection ~77 by 2050 and ~82 by 2100. World female advantage ~5 years.

wars.name: Battle of Kadesh and the Egyptian-Hittite war
wars.blurb: Pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought probably the largest chariot battle in history near Kadesh in Syria, and neither side won. The stalemate led to one of the oldest known peace treaties (about 1259 BCE), which kept the Levant stable for generations.

wars.name: Late Bronze Age collapse and the Sea Peoples
wars.blurb: Drought, earthquakes, broken trade routes and the raiders Egypt called the Sea Peoples brought down the Mycenaean palaces and the Hittite empire within a few decades. The collapse cleared the way for iron tools, new small states and the Phoenician alphabet.

wars.name: Neo-Assyrian conquests
wars.blurb: From Tiglath-Pileser III onward, Assyria's standing army conquered from Iran to Egypt, destroyed the kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE and deported whole populations. Its brutality united Babylonians and Medes, who sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE, and its system of provinces became the template for Persia.

wars.name: Conquests of Cyrus the Great and Cambyses
wars.blurb: Cyrus of Persia overthrew the Medes, took Lydia around 547 BCE and Babylon in 539 BCE, and his son Cambyses added Egypt in 525 BCE. The result was the largest empire yet, and Cyrus let exiled Judeans return home, which shaped the later Hebrew Bible.

wars.name: Greco-Persian Wars
wars.blurb: A revolt of Greek cities in Ionia drew Persia into war with mainland Greece. Victories at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea kept the Greek city-states independent, and Athens used its allies' tribute to build a naval empire, deepen its democracy and raise the Parthenon.

wars.name: Peloponnesian War
wars.blurb: Athens and Sparta fought for 27 years; a plague killed perhaps a quarter of Athenians and the Sicilian expedition destroyed their fleet. Persian gold helped Sparta win, but the exhausted Greek cities later fell under Macedon's control.

wars.name: Conquests of Alexander the Great
wars.blurb: In eleven years Alexander of Macedon destroyed the Persian Empire and marched to the Indus. His successors' kingdoms spread Greek language, cities and science from Egypt to Afghanistan, creating the Hellenistic world that Rome later absorbed.

wars.name: Punic Wars
wars.blurb: Rome and Carthage fought three wars for the western Mediterranean, and Hannibal's invasion of Italy killed a large share of Rome's young men. Rome's victory, ending with Carthage's destruction in 146 BCE, made it the Mediterranean superpower.

wars.name: Kalinga War
wars.blurb: Emperor Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga on India's east coast killed about 100,000 people by his own account. His remorse turned him toward Buddhism and non-violence, and the missionaries he sponsored helped spread Buddhism across Asia.

wars.name: Late Warring States and Qin unification
wars.blurb: The state of Qin defeated its rivals, reportedly massacring surrendered Zhao soldiers after Changping in 260 BCE, and unified China in 221 BCE. Qin's standard script, weights, laws and roads created the imperial state that later dynasties inherited.

wars.name: Roman civil wars (Social War to Actium)
wars.blurb: Six decades of civil war, from the Social War through Sulla, Caesar and Mark Antony, destroyed the Roman Republic. After Octavian won at Actium in 31 BCE and Ptolemaic Egypt fell in 30 BCE, he ruled as Augustus, founding the Roman Empire and two centuries of Pax Romana.

wars.name: Yellow Turban rebellion and Three Kingdoms wars
wars.blurb: Rebellion and the wars among Wei, Shu and Wu split Han China for nearly a century. Registered population fell by tens of millions, partly from war, famine and disease and partly from collapsed record keeping, until the Jin dynasty briefly reunited China in 280.

wars.name: Migration Period and fall of the Western Roman Empire
wars.blurb: Pushed by the Huns, Goths and other Germanic peoples crossed the Roman frontier, sacked Rome in 410 and 455, and deposed the last western emperor in 476. Their successor kingdoms, especially the Franks, became the seedbeds of medieval Europe while the eastern empire endured.

wars.name: Byzantine-Sasanian War of 602-628
wars.blurb: The last and greatest war between Rome's eastern empire and Persia swung from Persian armies at the walls of Constantinople to Emperor Heraclius sacking Persian palaces. It left both empires bankrupt and depopulated just before the Arab armies arrived.

wars.name: Early Muslim conquests
wars.blurb: Within a century of Muhammad's death, Arab armies conquered Persia, Byzantine Syria and Egypt, North Africa, Visigothic Spain and Sindh, and were turned back at Constantinople and in France. The caliphate linked old centers of learning and trade, later carrying paper-making and Indian numerals westward.

wars.name: An Lushan Rebellion
wars.blurb: A frontier general's revolt against the Tang dynasty wrecked northern China for eight years. Registered population collapsed (how much was death and how much was lost records is debated), and the weakened Tang ceded power to regional warlords as China's economic center shifted south.

wars.name: Viking Age raids and conquests
wars.blurb: Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers struck from Lindisfarne in 793 to Paris, Seville and Constantinople, and settled Iceland, Normandy, eastern England and the rivers of Russia. Their pressure helped unify England, and their trade routes linked the Baltic to Byzantium and Baghdad.

wars.name: Norman conquest of England
wars.blurb: In 1066 England beat a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, then fell to William of Normandy at Hastings, followed by the brutal Harrying of the North. Norman rule tied England to France, reshaped the English language and built the centralized state recorded in the Domesday Book.

wars.name: Crusades
wars.blurb: Called by the popes, western European armies fought for two centuries to win and hold Jerusalem, and the Fourth Crusade sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204. The crusades enriched Italian trading cities, fatally weakened Byzantium and left lasting distrust between the Christian and Muslim worlds.

wars.name: Mongol conquests
wars.blurb: Genghis Khan and his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary, killing perhaps 20 to 60 million people; storms wrecked their invasions of Japan. The Pax Mongolica then opened the Silk Road to merchants like Marco Polo, and probably to the plague that became the Black Death.

wars.name: Hundred Years' War
wars.blurb: English kings fought French kings for the French crown for over a century, through Crecy, Agincourt and Joan of Arc. Longbows and cannon undermined armored knights, and the long struggle helped forge separate English and French national identities.

wars.name: Conquests of Timur
wars.blurb: The Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur sacked cities from Baghdad to Delhi (1398) and crushed the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402. That defeat delayed the Ottoman capture of Constantinople by half a century, and his descendant Babur later founded India's Mughal Empire.

wars.name: Fall of Constantinople
wars.blurb: Sultan Mehmed II's giant cannons battered the walls of Constantinople until it fell in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, the last direct continuation of Rome. The Ottomans became a European power, and Greek scholars fleeing west helped feed the Italian Renaissance.

wars.name: Spanish conquest of the Americas
wars.blurb: After Columbus's 1492 voyage, Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec (1521) and Inca (1532-1572) empires. Most of the tens of millions who died were killed by Old World diseases such as smallpox, and American silver and crops like maize and potatoes transformed the world economy.

wars.name: Thirty Years' War
wars.blurb: A religious revolt in Bohemia grew into a European war fought mostly in Germany, which lost perhaps a fifth of its people to fighting, famine and plague (4.5 to 8 million died in all). The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 set up the system of sovereign states that still underlies international law.

wars.name: Ming-Qing transition
wars.blurb: Rebellion, famine and a Little Ice Age climate crisis brought down the Ming dynasty; Manchu armies took Beijing in 1644 and the last resistance on Taiwan in 1683. The Qing dynasty that followed greatly expanded China's borders and ruled until 1912.

wars.name: English Civil War (Wars of the Three Kingdoms)
wars.blurb: Conflicts between King Charles I, Parliament, Scotland and Ireland ended with the king's execution in 1649, with Ireland suffering the heaviest losses. The outcome, confirmed by the Glorious Revolution of 1688, established that the monarch rules with Parliament's consent, a principle behind later constitutional democracies.

wars.name: Seven Years' War
wars.blurb: Sometimes called the first world war, it was fought in Europe, North America, India and at sea. Britain won Canada and control of Bengal, but its war debts led to new taxes on American colonists, and France's losses fed the crisis behind its revolution.

wars.name: American Revolutionary War
wars.blurb: Thirteen British colonies rebelled over taxation and self-rule, declared independence in 1776 and won with French and Spanish help. The new republic's constitution and ideas of rights inspired revolutions in France and Latin America, while France's war debts hastened its own crisis.

wars.name: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars
wars.blurb: Revolutionary France fought coalitions of European monarchies, and Napoleon's mass conscript armies conquered most of the continent before failing in Russia (1812) and at Waterloo (1815). The wars ended the Holy Roman Empire, spread legal equality and nationalism, and left Britain the leading world power.

wars.name: Opium Wars
wars.blurb: Britain went to war to force China to accept opium imports and open its ports, later joined by France, and British troops burned Beijing's Old Summer Palace in 1860. The defeats began China's century of humiliation, weakened the Qing and helped spark the Taiping Rebellion.

wars.name: Taiping Rebellion
wars.blurb: A failed civil-service candidate who believed he was Jesus's younger brother led a rebellion that held much of southern China for over a decade. Some 20 to 30 million died, mostly of famine and disease, and the Qing survived only by relying on regional armies that later helped end the dynasty.

wars.name: American Civil War
wars.blurb: Eleven slave states seceded after Lincoln's election, and four years of war killed about 750,000 soldiers, about one in twelve white men of military age and nearly one in five in the South. Union victory ended slavery and made the United States a single industrial nation.

wars.name: World War I
wars.blurb: An assassination in Sarajevo pulled Europe's alliance systems into an industrial war of trenches, machine guns and gas. About 20 million died, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires collapsed, and the harsh peace set the stage for the next world war.

wars.name: Russian Civil War
wars.blurb: After the 1917 revolutions, the Bolshevik Reds fought the Whites, national movements and foreign interventions, while famine and epidemics killed far more than battle. The Red victory created the Soviet Union, whose one-party model and rivalry with the West shaped the rest of the century.

wars.name: World War II
wars.blurb: Nazi Germany's conquests in Europe and Japan's war in Asia (under way in China since 1937) became the deadliest conflict in history, including the Holocaust and the first atomic bombs. The outcome led to the United Nations, the US-Soviet Cold War and the end of European colonial empires.

wars.name: Korean War
wars.blurb: North Korea's invasion of the South drew in a US-led UN force and then Chinese armies, ending in stalemate near the original border. The war militarized the Cold War and left Korea divided, with South Korea later becoming an industrial democracy.

wars.name: Vietnam War
wars.blurb: The United States backed South Vietnam against the communist North and Viet Cong insurgents, with over 500,000 American troops there at the peak. Saigon fell in 1975 and Vietnam was reunified under communist rule, and the defeat changed American politics and its willingness to fight wars abroad.

wars.name: Afghanistan and Iraq wars
wars.blurb: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, US-led coalitions invaded Afghanistan and, in 2003, Iraq. Hundreds of thousands died, Iraq's turmoil fed the rise of ISIS, and the Taliban retook Afghanistan in 2021 as the last US troops left.

wars.name: Russian invasion of Ukraine
wars.blurb: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 became Europe's largest war since 1945, with deaths estimated in the hundreds of thousands (ongoing and highly uncertain as of 2024). It re-armed Europe, brought Finland and Sweden into NATO and disrupted world food and energy markets.

notes: worldPopulation: HYDE 3.3 / Gapminder / UN WPP 2024 series as published by Our World in Data (1000-year steps before 1 CE), rounded to 4 significant figures; 2024 is the UN WPP 2024 mid-year estimate. Pre-1800 values are reconstructions with wide error bars (other estimates for 1 CE range from about 170 to 300 million). birthRatePer1000: 1950-2023 from UN WPP 2024 via Our World in Data (note the 1959-1961 dip from China's Great Leap famine and the 1963 baby-boom peak); 2024 is a projection. Pre-1950 values are estimates consistent with near-stationary populations (crude birth rate roughly equals crude death rate, about 1000/e0, plus a small growth margin). lifeTables: both-sex survival l(x)/l(0) generated from a Siler-type hazard (falling juvenile hazard + constant background + Gompertz old-age hazard) fitted per era to target e0 and infant/child survival, cross-checked against Coale-Demeny West model life tables and historical tables; trapezoid e0 from the 22-point grid is within 0.1 year of the stated e0. Values after 1800 are blended world averages tilted toward the European, US and East Asian streams drawn in the blue layer, not the table of any one country. Low pre-modern e0 comes mainly from infant and child deaths: adults who reached 15 typically lived into their 40s-60s. femaleE0Advantage is female minus male e0 in years. wars: deaths are rounded totals (military and civilian, including war-driven famine and disease) from the Wikipedia list of wars by death toll and standard references (e.g. Hacker 2011 for the US Civil War, the Costs of War project for Iraq/Afghanistan). Tolls before about 1500 are order-of-magnitude guesses; Chinese tolls for the Three Kingdoms and An Lushan are census-derived and probably overstated; most Spanish-conquest deaths were from epidemics. maleExcessMortality is a rough blended fraction of military-age men of the listed civs killed over the whole war; where the burden differed widely, the optional maleExcessByCiv map (covering every listed civ) gives per-civ values and should be preferred (e.g. WWII USSR 0.2, Germany 0.25, US 0.013; Mongol conquests China 0.12 but Japan 0.001). Each war lists only civ streams active during its years. holy_roman_empire stands for Germany/Austria after 1806 and romans for Byzantium after 476. Legendary wars (e.g. Troy) are omitted. usGenerations: Pew Research Center boundaries (Greatest and Alpha boundaries vary by source; Alpha is open-ended). sexRatioAtBirth: the biological norm of about 105 boys per 100 girls; sex-selective abortion pushed China and India higher (about 1.10-1.17) from the 1980s.
